name: ESP32 dev board, ESP-WROOM-32 (3-pack)
why: The brain + the Wi-Fi access point. The Hack Pack's Arduino Nano cannot do this - it has no Wi-Fi radio at all, so this is the one thing that must be bought.

name: DRV8833 dual motor driver (6-pack)
why: The ESP32's pins can't drive motors. This chip does, both motors, both directions.

name: Mini DC motors 3-12V with brackets + props (6 sets)
why: 2 mm shaft, 24 mm can. Bought mainly for the MOUNTING BRACKETS - scavenged motors have nowhere to bolt to.

name: 80 mm 4-blade props, 2 mm shaft (20-pack)
why: The kit's little fan leaves are wind-turbine blades, not thrust props. These actually push air - and the extra diameter is what makes 5V from a power bank enough.

name: 400-point breadboards (4-pack)
why: Bench testing only. A breadboard on a moving boat shakes its wires out - solder before it goes in the water.

name: Dupont jumper wires, 120 pcs
why: Wire it up with no soldering the first time.

name: USB-C power bank
why: FREE - already own it (CrunchLabs Hack Pack ships one with each build). Regulated 5V, so the ESP32 can never brown out. This replaced the whole $43 battery + charger + holder stack.

name: USB-C to micro-USB cables (2-pack)
why: The ESP32's plug is micro-USB, the bank is USB-C. Cable 1 powers (and programs) the ESP32. Cable 2 gets its micro end cut off: red = +5V to the driver's VCC, black = GND. Must be C-to-micro, not C-to-A - a USB-C bank only turns its power on when the cable says a device is attached.

name: 220 ohm resistors (a few; any 150-330 ohm works)
why: One per LED. Without it the LED pulls too much current and burns out in a second.

name: Red, green, yellow LEDs
why: Navigation lights: red on port (left), green on starboard (right), yellow on the stern blinks while waiting for the tablet. Judges like a real-boat detail.

name: Lever wire clips (3)
why: Join the thin motor leads to jumper wires with no solder. Fold the bare end over so it's thick enough to grip, then tug-test it.

name: Soldering iron (only if you don't have one)
why: The motor driver comes with its pins loose. They have to be soldered into its 12 holes, or it won't make reliable contact in the breadboard. It's the only soldering in the build.

name: 63/37 rosin-core solder 0.8 mm + tip tinner
optional_note: if the kit's lead-free solder won't stick
why: The solder that came with the iron kit (tin-copper, lead-free) melts at 227 C and beads up instead of sticking. 63/37 melts at 183 C and flows easily, which makes it the beginner-friendly choice. Tip tinner revives a tip that has gone black. It contains lead, so wash hands after and no snacks at the bench.

name: Dry box: clamp-lid or screw-top food container
why: FREE - nothing on this boat is submerged, so the box only has to beat splash and one capsize. A clear kitchen container with a gasket lid does that.

name: Hull: 2L bottles, corrugated sign board, hot glue
why: Recycled - free, and it's a judged category.

name: Prop guards (craft mesh / splatter screen)
why: Two spinning props at kid height. Non-negotiable.

name: Marine silicone or hot glue for the wire holes
why: Two motor wires leave the box. That is the only hole in the system - seal it and strain-relieve it.

name: 1000 uF capacitor
optional_note: only if the bank cuts out
why: Optional: if the power bank trips on motor start-up, one capacitor across its 5V output smooths the spike. Salvage one from any dead electronics.

name: 8xAA battery holder with ON/OFF switch + leads (already owned)
why: The motor battery. Red lead to the driver's VCC, black to GND (tied to the ESP32's GND). Load 6 AA + 2 dummy cells (a wooden dowel wrapped in foil, or a wire joining the two springs) = 9 V. NEVER 8 real AA: 12 V breaks the driver (limit 10.8 V). 8 NiMH rechargeables = 9.6 V also works but is close. The switch is a physical motor kill switch. The ESP32 stays on the power bank.
